clue.text: Flattery, of the " stern and wild " variety, is sweet

parts.note: to butter someone up is to flatter them, so flattery is butter

parts.words: of the " stern and wild " variety
parts.note: Scott's line 'O Caledonia! stern and wild' describes Scotland, so this variety is the Scotch kind

explanation.surface: A remark on flattery: the rugged Highland kind is the sweetest of all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O Caledonia! stern and wild' is from Walter Scott's Lay of the Last Minstrel, a description of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard toffee made from brown sugar and butter is a sweet, in the British sense of a confection.

clue.text: He had a fair head for heights at Niagara Falls

definitions.text: He had a fair head for heights at Niagara Falls

parts.words: He had a fair head for heights at Niagara Falls
parts.note: the French acrobat who crossed the Niagara gorge on a tightrope; his stage name begins with a word for fair-haired, so a 'fair head' is literally in his name

explanation.surface: A daredevil who kept a cool head crossing high above Niagara.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a fair head for heights' reads as an idiom for not being afraid of heights, but the name opens with BLOND, a fair head of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Blondin was the celebrated tightrope walker who crossed the Niagara gorge in 1859.

clue.text: Manoeuvres round, or by, the Needles ?

definitions.text: Manoeuvres round, or by, the Needles ?

parts.words: Manoeuvres round, or by, the Needles
parts.note: a yacht rounding the Needles zigzags against the wind; also short pins pushed in by hand, and loose stitches made with a needle

explanation.surface: Sailing directions for getting past the Needles rocks off the Isle of Wight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight, a sailing landmark. The word means both a sailing boat's zigzag turns into the wind and short pins or tacking stitches made by needles.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing boat changes course into the wind in turns, and the same word names short pins and temporary needle stitches.

clue.text: Cite Green as being uncommonly full of beans

indicators.note: uncommonly says the letters of the two words are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone praising a colleague called Green for unusual liveliness.
explanation.definitionFit: Being full of beans is a British idiom for lively and vigorous.

clue.text: Glut in eggs at Easter

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Overindulging in chocolate eggs at Easter.
explanation.definitionFit: To glut is to fill to excess, the same as to satisfy fully.

clue.text: Goosey Italian music-maker

parts.note: the small egg-shaped wind instrument whose Italian name means 'little goose'

explanation.surface: A silly Italian musician, goosey meaning foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goosey' suggests a silly person, but the instrument's Italian name literally means little goose, from its shape.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocarina is a vessel flute whose name comes from Italian for little goose.

clue.text: An example of the boat-builder's

parts.note: a single vessel he makes, and also his trade or skill

explanation.surface: Admiring one piece of a shipwright's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'boat-builder's' as 'boat-builder's skill' and the word is his trade; read the clue as one boat he has built and it is a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a boat and a trade or skill such as boat-building.

clue.text: Analogy of one tram-line to another

definitions.meaning: a comparison or likeness between two things
two rails running side by side at the same distance apart, never meeting

explanation.surface: Comparing two tram tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: A similar case used for comparison is a likeness; tram rails run side by side without meeting.

clue.text: Virgilian gown ?

parts.note: a loose 17th-century gown that shares its name with the Italian city where Virgil was born

explanation.surface: Asking what a Roman poet wore.
explanation.walkthrough: Virgil was born near the Italian city of that name, and a mantua is also a loose gown worn by women in the 17th and 18th centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: The mantua was a loose gown or overdress, named after the city of Virgil's birth.

clue.text: Players by the score

parts.note: musicians who play from a printed score, and who come in great numbers, twenty at a time

explanation.surface: Sportsmen judged by the result of the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' and 'score' suggest a sports team and its result; here they are musicians reading a score, and 'by the score' also means in large numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A large body of instrumental musicians plays from a written musical score.

clue.text: Flower of Damascus?

parts.note: a flower is read as something that flows, a river; Naaman praises the rivers of Damascus in 2 Kings 5:12

explanation.surface: Asking about a blossom grown in the Syrian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a crossword favourite for a river, something that flows. Abana and Pharpar are named in the Bible as the rivers of Damascus.
explanation.definitionFit: Abana is the biblical river flowing through Damascus, named by Naaman in the Book of Kings.

clue.text: Same again, Herb ?Just what the doctor ordered !

parts.note: DO is short for ditto, the same again
sage is a herb

explanation.surface: Someone asks Herb whether he'll have the same again, a drink that is just what the doctor ordered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name; it is the herb SAGE. DO (ditto) means the same again.
explanation.definitionFit: The amount of medicine a doctor prescribes is exactly what was ordered.

clue.text: It's characteristic of Diana to be absent-minded

parts.note: Di is short for Diana, and 'of Diana' is Di's
a characteristic is a trait

explanation.surface: Remarking that Diana is famously forgetful.
explanation.definitionFit: Distrait is a French loan meaning distracted or preoccupied.

clue.text: Altogether a subject of pride before the fall?

definitions.text: Altogether a subject of pride before the fall?

parts.words: Altogether a subject of pride before the fall?
parts.note: being in the altogether means wearing nothing, which Adam and Eve were unashamed of before the Fall in Eden

explanation.surface: The proverb that pride comes before a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the altogether' is British slang for naked. Adam and Eve felt no shame at being unclothed until the Fall, playing on 'pride goes before a fall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the altogether means being unclothed, the state of having no clothes on.

clue.text: Clue for " ward " is no help at all !

parts.note: the word ward is the word draw written backwards, so the clue to it reads ...

explanation.surface: A complaint about a useless clue for the word ward.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'ward' backwards and it is DRAW; that instruction, draw back, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A disadvantage or snag is something that hinders rather than helps.

clue.text: La Traviata's flower

parts.note: Verdi's opera comes from Dumas's play La Dame aux camélias, whose heroine wears this bloom

explanation.surface: Asking which flower features in Verdi's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Verdi's La Traviata is based on Dumas's La Dame aux camélias, the lady of the camellias.
explanation.definitionFit: The camellia is the flower worn by the heroine of Dumas's novel on which Verdi's opera rests.

clue.text: Implacable ones placated by this title?

definitions.text: Implacable ones placated by this title?

parts.words: Implacable ones placated by this title?
parts.note: the Furies were called 'the kindly ones' in Greek, a flattering name meant to appease them

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a polite form of address would soothe fierce enemies.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greeks avoided naming the Furies and called them the Kindly Ones, hoping to appease them; Aeschylus's play takes that title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eumenides, the Kindly Ones, is the euphemistic Greek name for the avenging Furies.

clue.text: Headlock deadlock for the Jarndyce beneficiaries

definitions.meaning: in boxing and wrestling, a hold with the opponent's head under one's arm
the court in which the endless lawsuit Jarndyce v Jarndyce in Dickens's Bleak House is stuck

explanation.surface: Wrestling holds and legal stalemate in Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: In Bleak House the case of Jarndyce v Jarndyce drags on in the Court of Chancery until legal costs eat the estate. 'In chancery' is also an old boxing term for a head held under the arm.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Court of Chancery handled the estate in Bleak House, and the word was boxing slang for a head-hold.

clue.text: Card game in which many have had their chips

definitions.meaning: a two-to-four-player game of capturing cards from the table, often spelt with two S's

definitions.text: in which many have had their chips
definitions.meaning: a gambling house where many gamblers have lost their stake, 'had their chips' meaning finished

explanation.surface: A card game where players lost their stakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had their chips' is British slang for being done for, as well as the gambler's counters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassino is a fishing card game, and a gambling house is where gamblers lose their counters.

clue.text: Hastened to proceed to the capital

parts.note: to hasten is to run, so hastened is ran
to proceed is to go on

explanation.surface: Hurrying on to the capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangoon (now Yangon) was the capital of Burma when this puzzle was set.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangoon was the capital city of Burma, now Myanmar, until 2005.

clue.text: Blamed for having been too easy going?

indicators.note: the letters have been let go too loosely, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone was blamed for being too lenient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Easy-going' reads as lax in character, but here it means walking at a gentle pace.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow relaxed pace, an easy gait.

clue.text: Poor Cinders ! How will she make out?

indicators.note: poor says the word is in a bad state, its letters disordered

explanation.surface: Pity Cinderella: how will she manage?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' looks like 'get on, manage'; it means perceive.
explanation.definitionFit: To make out something is to perceive or detect it.

clue.text: Hissing from the snake's head

parts.note: the snake's hiss, a sound of the letter s, which is also the first letter of snake

explanation.surface: A snake hissing.
explanation.walkthrough: A snake hisses, and its head, the letter S, is the hissing sound in speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibilant is a speech sound such as s or sh that has a hiss.

clue.text: The sportsman's a good one — if not good enough

definitions.text: The sportsman's a good one — if not good enough

parts.words: The sportsman's a good one — if not good enough
parts.note: a gracious player who takes defeat well; he was not good enough to win

explanation.surface: Praise for a sporting gentleman who came second.
explanation.walkthrough: A good sport is 'a good one' at accepting defeat, the stock phrase being a good loser.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who fails to win is beaten, and a sportsman is admired for taking it well.

clue.text: Little sister takes one back to the Union

indicators.note: takes says the next piece is attached to the end
back says the word one is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
sis is a short form of sister

explanation.surface: A young sister brings someone back to the trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' looks like a trade union; it is the Greek Cypriot campaign for union of Cyprus with Greece, and 'back' turns 'one' round.
explanation.definitionFit: Enosis was the campaign for political union of Cyprus with Greece.

clue.text: Point to the silver fish

annotationWithheld.why: 'Point to the silver fish' (5) for SPIKE: Point is spike, but no attested sense makes 'silver fish' SPIKE, and S + PIKE needs S for silver, which has no standard source; the parse is unconfirmed.

clue.text: Lake formed by a continental dam

definitions.meaning: a dam is an animal's mother, and continental points to the French word for mother, from mainland Europe

explanation.surface: A lake made by building a dam in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dam' looks like a barrier for water; here it is a mother animal, and continental points to French.
explanation.definitionFit: A mere is a small lake in English, and mère is French for mother, as a dam is a beast's mother.

clue.text: Pinches nothing, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: nix is slang for nothing

explanation.surface: A petty thief takes nothing, so it's said.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick is British slang for to steal, the same as to pinch.

clue.text: Motorist's refinement gets him past the green in one

parts.note: over can mean past or beyond
a golfer reaching the green in a single stroke from the tee plays one long drive

explanation.surface: A golfing motorist overshoots the green in one stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The green in one' is golf: a drive is the long tee shot. Overdrive was an extra gear for economical cruising.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra high gear fitted to a car's gearbox is a refinement for motorists.

clue.text: A Shelley creation — the victim of his own

definitions.text: A Shelley creation — the victim of his own

parts.words: A Shelley creation — the victim of his own
parts.note: the scientist in Mary Shelley's novel is destroyed by the monster he himself made

explanation.surface: A Romantic poet's work turning on its maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelley' suggests the poet Percy, but it is Mary Shelley; her scientist is a victim of his own creation.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Frankenstein is the scientist in Mary Shelley's novel, killed by the creature he built.
